newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Rexrodt laughs off resignation talk.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Rexrodt laughs off resignation talk.

text.p: German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt on Wednesday shrugged off speculation he was about to resign, saying political sniping would not stop him from doing his job.
Responding to a report in the Stern weekly that some of his colleagues in the Free Democrat Party (FDP) wanted him out, Rexrodt said: "I can't say anything to that, just laugh."
"That is political theatre," he told SAT1 television. "I'm not going to let snipers or overenthusiastic journalists stop me from doing my work."

Rexrodt, in office since 1993, has come under attack from his own party over his handling of industry subsidies and schemes to try to create jobs in ex-communist eastern Germany, where one adult in five is unemployed.

The FDP's own headquarters was besieged for days last week by miners protesting at government plans to cut aid for the coal industry. Rexrodt had argued for deep cuts, but was overridden by Chancellor Helmut Kohl who offered more cash for peace in the coalfields.
Rexrodt, 55, won the public backing of the FDP's top brass on Tuesday, when party general secretary Guido Westerwelle dismissed the resignation talk as "an empty rumour".

Party leader Wolfgang Gerhardt, named by Stern as a likely alternative to Rexrodt for the economy portfolio, also said he had no plans to take ministerial office before a general election in October 1998.
Calls from the FDP's wings for Rexrodt to go have been led by Juergen Moellemann -- Rexrodt's predecessor as Economics Minister.
Moellemann, who is also FDP chairman in the coal-and-steel state of North Rhine-Westphalia, told Stern that it was vital for Gerhardt to join the cabinet.
Reports of Rexrodt's imminent departure triggered speculation by one heavyweight daily that Kohl would reshuffle his cabinet before the 1998 general election campaign.
Die Welt said that a likely cabinet shakeup would follow a formal announcement by Kohl, expected by some this spring, that he will stand for a record fifth term next year.

"Helmut Kohl has always indicated in public that he is not considering a reshuffle," Die Welt wrote. "But it is undisputed among coalition leaders that, once the Chancellor announces he will stand again, there must be personnel changes by autumn."

Sources close to Kohl told Reuters he had no plans at the moment to rejig his ministerial team. The issue was not discussed by Christian Democrat (CDU/CSU) leaders at a strategy meeting on Tuesday evening.

The sources did not, however, rule out ministerial changes this autumn as the Post Ministry will be abolished by the year's end. They also noted Kohl had reshuffled his cabinet a year before the 1994 elections.
The FDP is likely to seek ways of sharpening its profile in order to make sure that its 14-year-old alliance with Kohl remains intact beyond the next election.
The FDP is teetering in opinion polls just above the five percent threshold which it must cross to re-enter parliament under Germany's system of proportional representation.
